content.thinking:
I notice the error rate actually fell rather than rose, so the real impact was latency, not errors. The restart mitigation was logged at 07:58:04, but recovery in the metrics appears at 07:58:00 — meaning the timing suggests correlation rather than confirmed causation, so I should flag that as an assumption. I also need to be careful not to present the given figures as though I calculated them myself.

Root cause traces back to slow responses from the internal pricing dependency, with basket-total calls stretching to roughly 1500ms and spreading until nearly all requests were affected — no deploy or flag change happened on io-shop itself. I should list my key assumptions clearly: the restart's causal role is unconfirmed, io-pricing's own internals were never investigated, errors stayed at baseline so this was purely a latency issue, only a short window of logs and a 24-hour change search were reviewed (which doesn't rule out changes on io-pricing's side), and the proposed fix in the draft PR hasn't been reviewed or merged yet.

assumptions: That the restart of io-pricing is what fixed it is an assumption, not a finding. The metrics show recovery at 07:58, and the restart was issued at 07:58:04 — so the service was already back at baseline at or before the moment of the action. The restart was marked 'confirmed' on the basis that the service looked healthy afterwards, which is consistent with the restart working and equally consistent with the slowness having passed on its own.

The underlying fault inside io-pricing was never diagnosed. Only io-shop's metrics, logs and change history were examined; io-pricing's own telemetry, deploys and configuration were not. A restart without a known cause does not rule out recurrence.

The conclusion that the fault arrived from outside io-shop rests on finding no deploys, releases or flag changes for io-shop in the prior 24 hours. Changes to io-pricing in that window were not checked.
Only the 8 minutes of logs before the alert were read, so any earlier onset of upstream slowness would not have been visible.
Customer impact is inferred from latency and error-rate metrics rather than from any direct signal of abandoned sessions or lost baskets, even though the recorded errors are client disconnects.
The draft pull request is an unreviewed proposal; it is assumed to address the dependency's slowness but has not been validated.
input.executive_summary: For a short window on the morning of 28 September, the shop's account pages were slow to load. The cause was a slow internal service that the shop calls to price a shopper's basket; each of those calls took about a second and a half, and within a minute nearly every page view was waiting on one. Customers would have seen pages that loaded sluggishly rather than pages that failed — the share of failed requests during the window was no higher than normal, and the errors that did appear were shoppers closing the connection, at the same rate seen before the incident began. The automated responder picked up the alert within seconds, identified the slow dependency, and restarted it. Metrics show the service back at its normal latency at the end of the window, and the responder then closed the incident as mitigated. A draft code change has been opened for engineers to review; no permanent fix is in place yet.
input.root_cause: io-shop's latency rose because its internal pricing dependency (pricing.io-internal.svc / io-pricing) began answering /v1/shoppers/.../basket-total calls in about 1500ms — affecting a quarter of requests in the first minute and then essentially every request — so io-shop's account-page renders blocked on a slow upstream. Nothing changed in io-shop itself: no deploys or releases in the preceding 24 hours and no recent feature-flag changes, which is why the fault was attributed to the dependency rather than to io-shop. Why io-pricing turned slow was never established; the investigation stopped at io-shop's own logs and metrics.
